title: UK film and high-end TV: competitive strengths, fragile pipelines
label: 11 November 2026 · British film and high-end television follow-up
summary: Witnesses and ministers agreed the UK remains a world-leading place to make film and high-end TV — great talent, facilities and inward investment — but the sector is fragile. The session focused on tax incentives and finance for UK stories, distribution and exhibition, support for freelancers and skills, AI and copyright risks, regional commissioning, and culture change to prevent misconduct. Ministers were urged to press Treasury on targeted reliefs and to speed up practical support for freelancers, AI guidance, and regional growth.

glossary.definition: A UK tax incentive introduced in 2024 that helps pay for independent British films by reducing producers' tax bills.
A broadcaster (like the BBC) whose remit includes serving public interests such as regional commissioning and training.
BFI funding to help British film and TV reach international markets; its UK distribution has recently increased.
A proposed tax credit to encourage marketing and cinema releases of independent films to help them reach audiences.
An industry body and reporting service set up to handle misconduct allegations and improve standards in screen production.

chapters.title: Where the sector stands now
chapters.takeaway: UK film and high-end TV are world-class, with box office recovering, but production is under pressure from global competition and weaker domestic commissioning.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Harriet, briefly: where is the sector now compared with our April 2025 report?

turns.speaker: Harriet Finney
turns.text: UK box office is back to pre‑COVID levels — about 100 million admissions — helped by a couple of big films. But production is dipping: commissioning worldwide has fallen and other countries are getting more competitive with incentives.

turns.speaker: Claire Mundell
turns.text: Financing remains the critical pinch point. The mid-tier British cultural stories—regional projects and £1m–£3m dramas—are hardest to fund.

turns.speaker: Pete Johnson
turns.text: Long term demand for audiovisual content is big, but many countries have boosted spend. We must protect our competitiveness—skills, tax, and infrastructure—so our share grows, not shrinks.

chapters.title: Tax reliefs and finance — what’s working and what’s missing
chapters.takeaway: New independent film tax relief helps, but witnesses want R&D credits, distribution incentives, and targeted support for mid-tier TV; ministers say Treasury decides tax policy but are open to evidence.

turns.speaker: Dr Huq
turns.text: Did the independent film tax credit (IFTC) deliver and are smaller companies seeing benefits?

turns.speaker: Harriet Finney
turns.text: IFTC has helped make films that wouldn’t otherwise get made—about 400 projects certified so far—but the formal impact assessment will appear in our 2027 report because we need more data.

turns.speaker: Pete Johnson
turns.text: IFTC is helping, but we also need more risk capital for indie companies, and a distribution tax credit so those films reach cinemas. That credit was projected to pay back to the Treasury.

turns.speaker: Claire Mundell
turns.text: R&D relief is vital for indie producers to finance development. Broadcaster development funding is down, which dries the pipeline for future projects.

turns.speaker: Nigel Huddleston
turns.text: Are tax incentives really pivotal, or would our talent and studios suffice without them?

turns.speaker: Claire Mundell
turns.text: No. Producers follow the money—if incentives aren’t competitive, projects and talent go where the incentives are.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Minister, are you pressing Treasury for a £1m–£3m high-end TV uplift and other changes?

turns.speaker: Ian Murray
turns.text: We keep tax reliefs under review and back the sector’s evidence. Final decisions are for the Treasury. Officials talk to Treasury; I personally met the Treasury Minister once this year to press the case.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The Committee expected more active ministerial advocacy on this.

chapters.title: Distribution, domestic production and the BBC’s role
chapters.takeaway: Inward investment dominates UK production; witnesses warn domestic stories risk being filmed abroad; the BBC and lottery funds are central to keeping regional and low‑budget stories alive.

turns.speaker: Pete Johnson
turns.text: In 2025 about 91% of film production in the UK was inward investment. That brings jobs, but our domestic sector is small and vulnerable to other countries’ incentives.

turns.speaker: Gill German
turns.text: If lottery distribution changes, what’s at risk for the BFI and grassroots film activities?

turns.speaker: Harriet Finney
turns.text: Lottery funding supports talent development, small British stories and audiences. We fund 2,000 cinemas and festivals; without it many regional and low-budget projects wouldn’t get made.

turns.speaker: Alison Hume
turns.text: How do we stop inward investment from crowding out the home-grown dramas that reflect UK life?

turns.speaker: Ian Murray
turns.text: It’s not either/or. Inward investment brings GVA and jobs, while PSBs like the BBC support domestic stories; charter review will set clearer expectations for PSB spend and regional production.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You say Treasury decides tax changes. How many times have you personally pressed Treasury on the £1m–£3m ask?

turns.speaker: Ian Murray
turns.text: Once this year. Officials liaise frequently, and we continue to make the case.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The Committee felt that was not enough.

chapters.title: Freelancers, skills and regional supply chains
chapters.takeaway: Freelancers are the sector’s backbone but face worklessness, weak data, and limited training; Government set Freelance Champions and funds, but practical data collection and apprenticeship fit remain urgent tasks.

turns.speaker: Jo Stevens
turns.text: What should the Freelance Champions prioritise to help freelancers now?

turns.speaker: Pete Johnson
turns.text: Jobs are scarce now: many freelancers have considered leaving. Champions should map work patterns, pay and support systems, and look at models used abroad to smooth freelancer incomes.

turns.speaker: Claire Mundell
turns.text: Freelancers are the engine room. We need stable commissioning and business terms so companies can plan and offer work. Otherwise skills leave the sector.

turns.speaker: Mr Alaba
turns.text: Harriet, what about the BFI impact assessment and the mid‑tier HETV relief idea?

turns.speaker: Harriet Finney
turns.text: We’ll publish the independent film tax relief assessment in our screen business report next year. We’re working with industry on where incentives could be optimised for domestic growth.

turns.speaker: Jo Stevens
turns.text: Who is collecting the freelancers and skills data to make the levy and apprenticeships fit such a project-based sector?

turns.speaker: Ian Murray
turns.text: It’s complicated across Departments. The Freelance Champions will lead, supported by DCMS and the sector bodies, and we’ll bring together data from different government systems.

turns.speaker: Georgia Hutchinson
turns.text: We’re funding research and academic support for the Champions to pull government and industry data together and identify gaps.

chapters.title: AI, copyright, deepfakes and creative practice
chapters.takeaway: BFI is funding AI R&D and will publish guidance; the Government has four AI‑copyright workstreams (transparency, labelling, creator control, digital replicas) and plans consultation, but creators want faster clarity and protections.

turns.speaker: Liz Jarvis
turns.text: Has progress been made on protecting performers from voice cloning, deepfakes and using their work to train AI?

turns.speaker: Harriet Finney
turns.text: We welcomed Government moving away from an opt‑out for creators. BFI has invested £1.2m in AI R&D labs to give makers safe room to experiment; guidance and guard‑rails will follow next year.

turns.speaker: Pete Johnson
turns.text: Industry needs legal clarity so companies will invest. Our members are engaging with the IPO and Government on rules about training models and liability.

turns.speaker: Dr Huq
turns.text: ScreenSkills says 80% of roles could be affected by AI but 70% of the workforce has had no training. Will you meet unions and APPG groups worried about the risk?

turns.speaker: Ian Murray
turns.text: Yes. AI can help the sector but poses real job risks. We’ve appointed AI champions and set up four copyright workstreams; I’ll meet the groups you name to hear concerns and priorities.

turns.speaker: Georgia Hutchinson
turns.text: The consultation will look at consent and the difference between big‑budget uses and vulnerable early‑career performers being asked for footage for future AI use.

chapters.title: Culture, misconduct and final asks
chapters.takeaway: Industry and Government back stronger reporting, CIISA and training to change culture and protect vulnerable people; ministers will convene the sector and consider NDA misuse alongside wider charter and regulatory work.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How are you tackling cultural abuse in the sector and the misuse of NDAs?

turns.speaker: Ian Murray
turns.text: The Government will convene the sector and push for zero tolerance. NDAs are a problem when used to silence victims; we must ensure whistleblowers can come forward safely.

turns.speaker: Pete Johnson
turns.text: CIISA now exists and an industry reporting service opened last month. Many companies are changing HR, reporting and training, but culture change takes time.

turns.speaker: Claire Mundell
turns.text: On the ground, productions now have mandatory training and safeguarding reps. More vigilance and consistent standards are still needed.

turns.speaker: Harriet Finney
turns.text: Final ask: don’t be complacent. Keep pushing the outstanding recommendations on incentives, the BBC funding settlement and lottery support—these underpin diversity of British stories and workforce development.

turns.speaker: Ian Murray
turns.text: Final word from government: we back the sector, it’s a national jewel, and we’ll keep working on tax, skills, AI and culture. We welcome the Committee’s scrutiny as we refine policy.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all. The Committee will press on the points you raised, especially incentives, distribution and urgent support for freelancers and regional production.
